item.title: Lindblad Multiproduct Formulas
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Lindblad Multiproduct Formulas (L-MPF) combine classically computed linear coefficients with noisy quantum expectation values to outperform low-bond-dimension classical tensor network simulations and unmitigated quantum results on 65 qubits, achieving classical GPU speedups up to 5.6×.

Grade 0.384 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling” · Niall F. Robertson, Andrea D'Urbano, Anton Dekusar, Max Rossmannek, Eric D. Switzer, James R. Garrison, Nicolas Lorente, Igor Pasichnyk, Paolo D'Alberto, Muhammad Osama, Zachary Streeter, Yasuko Eckert, Constantinos Evangelinos, Sergiy Zhuk

Figure

Expectation value vs. Floquet cycle number, comparing purely classical low-bond simulations, unmitigated hardware measurements, and L-MPF error-mitigated results against high-bond-dimension classical ground truth.

Asks

Can high-dimensional tensor network contractions be integrated directly into a quantum error mitigation workflow to estimate noiseless expectation values with rigorous error bars?

But

Demonstrated on a 2D discrete time crystal model on a 3×3 heavy-hexagonal lattice up to 10 Floquet cycles; non-ergodic amplification settings require PEA and higher sample counts to prevent large error bars.

Tools

Lindblad Multiproduct Formulas (L-MPF) · Loop-corrected belief propagation · 2D tensor networks · Ergodic amplification / Probabilistic error amplification · ibm_basquecountry quantum processor (65 qubits)

Abstract

We introduce Lindblad Multiproduct Formulas: a quantum error mitigation technique that uses two-dimensional tensor networks contracted with loop-corrected belief propagation. The quantities required to implement the error mitigation scheme that are evaluated with tensor networks can be less computationally expensive to calculate than the expectation values themselves, thus allowing for the possibility of applying our method to certain systems for which tensor network methods may struggle to calculate the observable quantities of interest. The workflow incorporates Clifford rescaling techniques and outputs an estimated error bar. We apply our method to a model of two-dimensional discrete time crystals studied previously and implement it on 65 qubits arranged in a 3 ×3 heavy-hexagonal topology on the quantum computer ibm_basquecountry. We show that a GPU implementation of the classical part of our workflow achieves a speedup of up to 5.6×.

item.title: DPRQ: A Dynamic Programming-based Qubit Routing Algorithm for Collective Communication in Distributed Quantum Computing
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Dynamic programming qubit routing reduces inter-node EPR pair consumption by an average of 24.40% and up to 85.06% across 80 circuit configurations.

Grade 0.372 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Dhaval Vaidya (North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA), Ruozhou Yu (North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA)

Figure

EPR cost plotted against total circuit qubits (50 to 200) for DPRQ versus QuComm across four benchmark circuits. DPRQ maintains lower communication cost as network size increases.

Asks

How to minimize inter-node communication across collective communication blocks in distributed quantum circuits by accounting for global inter-block dependencies?

Before

QuComm compiler, which uses greedy block-level routing.

But

Evaluated on 4 benchmark circuits (QAOA, RCA, BV, VQE) up to 200 qubits in simulation across 3 network topologies (mesh-grid, ring, fully-connected).

Tools

dynamic programming · collective quantum communication · TP-Comm protocol · communication fusion · shortest-path early execution

Abstract

Distributed quantum computing (DQC) offers a promising approach to scale quantum computing by overcoming the resource limitations of a single quantum processor. However, inter-node communication remains a major bottleneck of DQC due to inefficient and error-prone entanglement distribution. Optimizing inter-node communication can not only reduce the amount of entanglement resource needed to execute a quantum circuit but also improve execution speed and accuracy of the results. This paper proposes DPRQ, a qubit routing algorithm for minimizing inter-node communication in distributed quantum circuits divided into collective communication blocks. Unlike current approaches that utilize greedy block-level qubit routing strategies, DPRQ employs a dynamic programming-based technique focused on global circuit-level optimization, while capturing inter-block dependencies. We evaluated DPRQ on four sets of quantum circuits and a variety of DQC configurations. The results demonstrate that DPRQ's innovative routing strategy achieves an average of 24.40% reduction with a maximum of 85.06% reduction in inter-node communication, when compared to the state-of-the-art collective communication-based DQC compiler QuComm.

item.title: Thermal lifetime of the centralized repetition code: From quantum annealing to social dynamics
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Centralized repetition code storage lifetime scales exponentially with qubit count n at any finite temperature T<∞, avoiding the thermal instability of a 1D Ising chain despite having only 1 Ising bond per qubit.

Grade 0.372 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Ari Mizel, Van Molino

Figure

Upper bound on the transition rate eigenvalue λ1 plotted against qubit number n at inverse temperature βJ=0.8. The decay toward zero illustrates exponentially increasing stability with system size even when thermal energy kBT exceeds coupling J.

Asks

Does a star-graph centralized repetition code behave thermodynamically like an unstable 1D Ising chain or a stable complete-graph repetition code under thermal noise?

But

Local bit-flip error model only (does not suppress phase errors). Assumes Born-Markov bath coupling and odd physical qubit number n.

Tools

Lindblad master equation · spectral analysis · variational eigenvalue bounds · Gershgorin circle theorem

Abstract

There is an extensive body of research probing the potential of adiabatic quantum computation and quantum annealing to solve hard computational problems. This research endeavor is complicated by noise afflicting hardware during the computational process. An error-correcting approach called quantum annealing correction (QAC) was suggested to mitigate this noise. The QAC approach employs a centralized version of the repetition code in which the qubits are configured in a star-graph pattern with one special qubit playing the role of the hub. In this paper, we explore the thermal physics of the centralized repetition code, using a Lindblad equation framework to analyze its lifetime when coupled to a thermal bath. We show that its centralized configuration leads to thermal stability, enabling the robust storage of a logical bit of information, despite the fact that there is only 1 ferromagnetic Ising interaction per qubit like a 1-dimensional Ising chain.

item.title: Toward Resilient Many-Body Formulations under Incomplete Correlation Models: A Dual-Space Variational Formulation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Dual-space NOCI variationally couples a parent reference manifold to generated correlated quantum states, bounding the Rayleigh–Ritz energy at or below both reference-only NOCI and correlated-only NOQE while reducing sensitivity to amplitude and matrix-element noise.

Grade 0.368 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Vibin Abraham, Bhumika Jayee, Bo Peng, Nicholas P. Bauman, Karol Kowalski

Figure

Energy error relative to FCI for linear H4 plotted against amplitude noise variance σ. DS-NOCI retains stable accuracy while correlated-only NOQE error degrades rapidly.

Asks

How can quantum subspace eigensolvers augment a classical nonorthogonal configuration interaction reference without degrading variational flexibility when correlated quantum states are incomplete or noisy?

But

Simulated benchmarks on small molecules (H2, H4, H6, N2, cyclobutadiene); noisy matrix elements degrade the strict variational bound without metric regularization.

Tools

Dual-space nonorthogonal configuration interaction (DS-NOCI) · Nonorthogonal quantum eigensolver (NOQE) · Rayleigh–Ritz variational diagonalization · Schur metric conditioning

Abstract

Quantum simulations of correlated many-body systems will inevitably operate with imperfect information: the prepared states may arise from incomplete or approximate ansatze, while their measured Hamiltonian and overlap matrix elements are additionally affected by hardware and statistical noise. Robust quantum algorithms will be those that can improve upon reliable lower-level descriptions in spite of these imperfections. We introduce a dual-space nonorthogonal configuration-interaction (DS-NOCI) framework built around this principle. Rather than replacing a classically accessible NOCI reference manifold with correlated quantum states, DS-NOCI retains both spaces and couples them variationally. The reference sector provides a stable many-body backbone, while the quantum states contribute whatever additional correlation directions they contain. With exact matrix elements, the enlarged dual space gives a ground-state energy no higher than either the reference-only NOCI or correlated-only quantum-NOCI spaces, ensuring that an incomplete correlation model cannot degrade the underlying variational description. The additional reference--correlated matrix elements require only one correlated state preparation and are therefore less demanding than the correlated--correlated block already required by quantum variant of NOCI. Molecular benchmarks further show enhanced resilience to imperfect amplitudes and noisy matrix elements. DS-NOCI thus provides a general strategy for building quantum many-body formulations that remain useful when both correlation models and quantum computations are necessarily incomplete and noisy.

item.title: State-Based Quantum Operations: Chameleon Gates
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Introduced chameleon gates 𝒞ρ parametrized by a quantum state knob ρ, constructible via a controlled-swap and partial trace to implement state-based quantum computation and simulate nonlinear Hamiltonians.

Grade 0.361 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling” · S. Alipour, A. T. Rezakhani

Figure

Circuit schematic for the chameleon gate 𝒞ρ and its implementation using an ancilla in state ψδ, a state knob ρ, target state σ, controlled-swap, and partial tracing over the first target.

Asks

How can quantum controlled-gates be generalized to adapt their transformations dynamically based on arbitrary input quantum states without prior knowledge of those states?

But

Requires ancilla control qubit initialized with small parameter |δ|≪1; valid up to O(δ2) error; requires post-selection on the |+⟩ measurement outcome.

Tools

Controlled-swap (Fredkin) gate · Partial trace · Post-selection · Trotter-Suzuki expansion

Abstract

We introduce chameleon gates as a natural generalization of conventional quantum controlled-gates. Chameleon gates are state-based quantum controlled-operations that retain standard elements such as control and target systems, while introducing a new feature: the quantum knob. This knob is a quantum signal (state) that determines the operation performed by the gate. Consequently, the action and form of a chameleon gate depend dynamically on the quantum knob, allowing the gate to adapt its operation and implement transformations that are not necessarily unitary. This shapeshifting property is in stark contrast to conventional quantum controlled-gates, whose actions are fixed and cannot be modified. We also propose how chameleon gates can be realized using conventional quantum gates available in current quantum technologies. We then employ chameleon gates as a useful building block within the recently proposed state-based quantum computation (SBQC) framework. Using this approach, we demonstrate the simulation of state-dependent (nonlinear) quantum evolutions.

item.title: Compiling the 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy estimation algorithm for active volume quantum architectures
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Active-volume-aware compilation cuts the active volume of 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy estimation by up to 3.9× across L×L square lattices with L=4 to 20. Also cuts Toffoli count by ∼2× at L=20.

Grade 0.340 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Harriet Apel, Athena Caesura, Carys Harvey, Sam Heavey, Angus Kan, Jessica Lemieux, Ryan Levy, Sam Pallister, Joseph Peetz, William Pol, Sukin Sim, William A. Simon, Mark Steudtner, Gideon Uchehara

Figure

Active volume and conventional computational spacetime volume plotted against logical qubit count across square lattice sizes L=4 to 20, comparing baseline against improved compilation.

Asks

How much can the execution cost and runtime of quantum phase estimation for 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy be reduced by compiling directly for active-volume architectures instead of non-Clifford proxies?

Before

Baseline compilation optimized for non-Clifford cost, as analyzed by Campbell (2022) and Kan et al. (2024).

But

Evaluated for t=1, u=8 with periodic boundary conditions and extensive energy error budget 0.0051tLxLy.

Tools

active-volume-aware compilation · second-order Suzuki-Trotter evolution · sine-window quantum phase estimation · batched Hamming weight phasing · oriented ZX calculus

Abstract

As quantum computing enters the early fault-tolerant era, circuit compilation choices will increasingly depend on details of the underlying architecture rather than solely optimizing for generic proxies such as non-Clifford count. We present an active-volume-aware compilation of the ground-state energy estimation algorithm for the two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model using quantum phase estimation and Trotterized time evolution. The proposed compilation reduces the active volume across L×L square lattices with L=4 to 20, achieving up to a 3.9× reduction over prior work optimized for non-Clifford cost. As a by-product of these compilation improvements, the resulting circuits also achieve state-of-the-art Toffoli counts, with a ~2× reduction for the L=20 case. Lastly, the active volume architecture and recent execution scheduling advances provide a means of translating these reduction trends into runtime. This demonstrates the increasing importance of architecture-aware compilation for practical early fault-tolerant quantum computing.

item.title: Ancilla mediated steady-state engineering in open quantum systems
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Demonstrated ancilla-mediated reservoir engineering on a solid-state spin pair, realizing anti-thermalization to a negative-temperature steady state and achieving quantum battery steady-state ergotropy exceeding 70% of theoretical maximum after 30 collisions.

Grade 0.337 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “thermalization, many-body localization and quantum scars in driven systems” · Soham Pal, Karen Hovhannisyan, Omri Porat, Shovan Dutta, Janet Anders, Helena Knowles

Figure

Excited-state population dynamics and energetics of the nuclear spin system qubit undergoing collisions under engineered interaction channels.

Asks

Can an ancilla qubit be used to engineer tunable system-reservoir coupling and reservoir temperature to achieve anti-thermalization and non-equilibrium steady states?

But

Natural 13C abundance Type IIa diamond at room temperature; NV-nuclear spin correlations assumed weak and ignored across cycle boundaries.

Tools

single NV center electron spin (ancilla) · proximal ¹³C nuclear spin (target system) · shaped Gaussian microwave pulses · 532 nm optical polarization and readout

Abstract

Engineering the properties of a reservoir and its coupling to a quantum system is a powerful tool for simulating quantum thermodynamic processes and for generating otherwise inaccessible steady states. Yet tailoring both the reservoir and its coupling within a single platform remains challenging. Here we introduce a platform, in which an ancilla qubit mediates the coupling of a target system to a reservoir, providing independent control over the interaction form, coupling strength, and effective reservoir temperature. Our implementation uses the electron spin of a single nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond as the ancilla and a proximal ¹³C nuclear spin as the target. By alternating engineered unitary interactions with dissipative ancilla resets, we realize dynamics naturally described by a collision model, enabling straight-forward tracking of the work, heat, coherence, and entropy generated at every collision. We experimentally demonstrate conventional thermalization and also realize anti-thermalization: the stabilization of the target system in a temperature opposite to that of its reservoir. Finally, harnessing this steady-state engineering, we utilize the nuclear spin as a quantum battery, achieving a steady-state ergotropy exceeding 70% of the theoretical maximum.

item.arxave:tools: single NV center electron spin (ancilla) · proximal ¹³C nuclear spin (target system) · shaped Gaussian microwave pulses · 532 nm optical polarization and readout
item.arxave:abstract: Engineering the properties of a reservoir and its coupling to a quantum system is a powerful tool for simulating quantum thermodynamic processes and for generating otherwise inaccessible steady states. Yet tailoring both the reservoir and its coupling within a single platform remains challenging. Here we introduce a platform, in which an ancilla qubit mediates the coupling of a target system to a reservoir, providing independent control over the interaction form, coupling strength, and effective reservoir temperature. Our implementation uses the electron spin of a single nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond as the ancilla and a proximal ¹³C nuclear spin as the target. By alternating engineered unitary interactions with dissipative ancilla resets, we realize dynamics naturally described by a collision model, enabling straight-forward tracking of the work, heat, coherence, and entropy generated at every collision. We experimentally demonstrate conventional thermalization and also realize anti-thermalization: the stabilization of the target system in a temperature opposite to that of its reservoir. Finally, harnessing this steady-state engineering, we utilize the nuclear spin as a quantum battery, achieving a steady-state ergotropy exceeding 70% of the theoretical maximum.

item.title: TETRIS-Q: Tiling-based Effective Transient-fault Reduction on Interleaved Superconducting Qubits
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Combining substrate phonon barrier tiling with QEC interleaving reduces peak logical error rate by over 99.8% and shortens transient duration by 80% under simulated radiation strikes. Sparser multi-qubit tiling cuts barrier fabrication perimeter cost by up to 87% with minimal performance loss.

Grade 0.331 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…” · Marzio Vallero, Gioele Casagranda, Flavio Vella, Paolo Rech

Figure

Heatmap of average logical error rate for a distance-7 rotated surface code across tile sizes (1 to 16 qubits) and numbers of interleaved codes (1 to 9) at barrier permeability bp=0.1.

Asks

Can substrate-level phonon barrier tiling and quantum error correction code interleaving mitigate radiation-induced spatially correlated faults in superconducting quantum chips without execution overhead?

But

Numerical simulation only (51 million circuit simulations) using rotated surface codes under a parametrizable barrier permeability model (bp).

Tools

TETRIS-Q planar-mesh tiling algorithm · rotated surface code simulation · substrate-level phonon barrier model · QEC code interleaving

Abstract

The struggle of the hour in quantum computing research is achieving effective suppression of the error mechanisms induced by the interaction of external radiation with superconducting quantum devices. Despite the rapid advancements in quantum error correction (QEC) of recent years, radiation-induced faults are yet to be fully addressed. These events are known to be the cause of simultaneous correlated defects in qubits that lie onto a single substrate, ultimately jeopardising QEC code effectiveness. In this paper, we propose to selectively combine substrate-level phonon barriers and QEC interleaving via a planar-mesh tiling algorithm, TETRIS-Q, reaching efficient and effective suppression of radiation events. Our cross-layer solution comes at no extra cost in terms of QEC code execution or decoding time. We model and simulate radiation-induced transient faults over a plethora of barrier and QEC interleaving configurations. Through more than 51 million quantum circuit simulations, we show peak logical error reductions of more than 99.8 %, together with an 80% reduction of the observable transient duration with permeable barriers. We find that sparser tiling can reach comparable performance to single qubit tiling, prompting cost reductions of upwards of 87 % in barrier tracing. By leveraging independent QEC code interleaving, we measure up to one order of magnitude average logical error rate reductions without the use of permeable barriers, and up to three orders of magnitude with the joint usage of barriers.
